lesson.title: O(log n): Logarithmic Time and the Power of Cutting Problems in Half
lesson.summary: An algorithm runs in logarithmic time, O(log n), when it reduces the problem size by a constant fraction, usually half, at every step, letting it handle huge inputs in relatively few operations.
lesson.body:
Logarithmic time, O(log n), is one of the most powerful growth rates in this unit, because it grows so slowly. An O(log n) algorithm does not need to look at most of its input at all. Instead, it repeatedly throws away a large fraction of the remaining possibilities at each step, which is why binary search is the textbook example of logarithmic time.

Binary search works on a sorted list by comparing the target to the middle element, then discarding half of the remaining list depending on whether the target is smaller or larger, and repeating.

def binary_search(sorted_values, target):
    low, high = 0, len(sorted_values) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if sorted_values[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif sorted_values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1

Every time through the loop, the range between low and high shrinks by roughly half. Starting from n elements, after one comparison at most n/2 elements remain to check, after two comparisons at most n/4 remain, after three at most n/8 remain, and so on. The question of how many times you can cut n in half before reaching 1 is exactly what the logarithm log2(n) answers. That is where the name comes from: the number of steps is proportional to log2(n).

This connects directly to why binary search needs a sorted list: cutting the search space in half only works because you can be certain which half the target must be in, by comparing it to the middle value. Linear search has no such guarantee on unsorted data, which is why it must fall back to checking elements one at a time, O(n), instead of eliminating half the remaining data at each step.

The doubling thought experiment shows exactly how slowly O(log n) grows. Suppose binary_search takes about 10 comparisons in the worst case to find a target in a sorted list of 1,024 elements, since 2 to the 10th power is 1024, so log2(1024) equals 10. Doubling the list to 2,048 elements adds only one more comparison, about 11, because log2(2048) equals 11. Doubling again to 4,096 elements needs only 12 comparisons. You could double the input size ten more times, reaching over a million elements, and still only need about 20 comparisons total. This is what makes O(log n) algorithms feel almost magical: enormous inputs barely slow them down.

Logarithmic time depends entirely on being able to eliminate a large chunk of the problem at each step without having to examine it. Binary search can do this because the list is sorted; other logarithmic algorithms, like searching a balanced binary tree, work for similar reasons. Whenever you see an algorithm's problem size getting cut by a constant fraction, usually in half, at each step, that is your signal to look for O(log n).
